What the public catalogue can see

Cycle 11dcd35c2c44, first seen 2026-09-09 20:34 UTC, scored 2026-09-09 21:56 UTC against the public catalogue snapshot fetched 2026-09-09 18:10 UTC (12,811 element sets).

At the first instant of each operator file, the public catalogue puts 79% of the scored Starlink satellites within 10 km of where the operator says they are. The middle satellite is 3.1 km away, with the public information a median of 9 hours old. Where the public information is two to three days old, the two predictions are about 31 km apart. Both sides are predictions, and most of that spread is planned trajectory changes the public catalogue cannot know about.

Everyone outside SpaceX sees Starlink through the public catalogue of orbital elements. Ephemera takes that public element set for each satellite, propagates it with SGP4, and compares it against the operator's own published trajectory for the same satellite at the same instants. The distance between the two is what this measures. It is not an error of the satellite, and it is not a statement about which side is right.

26 satellites (0.2%) are more than 1,000 km from the public prediction at publication, which is a large part of an orbit. For those the public element set is not on the operator's trajectory at all. Ephemera does not label any separation as a manoeuvre; that needs a detector this project has not built.

Element age is how old the public catalogue's information was at the instant compared. It runs larger than catalogue staleness because a single operator file predicts three days ahead, so a comparison late in the file is both further ahead and matched against an older element set. The two effects are not separated within one cycle, which is why the headline uses only the first instant of each file.

By altitude shell. The lowest shell is where satellites are being raised and lowered, so its spread is the widest.

Feed health for this cycle. 11,080 of 11,134 operator files scored. 54 have no entry in the public catalogue, of which 54 are new satellites the catalogue has not numbered yet; 0 marked decayed; 0 failed to propagate; 0 unreadable; 0 no longer matching the record. Public element sets were a mean of 11.5 h old when the snapshot was taken (median 8.8 h, 90th percentile 21.5 h, 6 over 72 h). Averaged over every comparison, which run out to three days into the operator file, element age is 47.7 h: the difference is the file's own prediction horizon, not catalogue staleness. Space-Track: 78 snapshots held, last fetched 2026-09-10 00:10 UTC with 12,811 element sets. Poller heartbeat coverage over the last 24 h: 74.3%.

How this was measured

Public element set (Space-Track gp snapshot) propagated with SGP4 (skyfield 1.55, python-sgp4 2.27; TEME to GCRS by Skyfield, taken as J2000) and differenced against the operator-published trajectory (EME2000) at the file's own record epochs every 360 min. Distance in km; components in the operator's radial/in-track/cross-track frame; altitude is geocentric radius minus 6378.137 km; element age is evaluation epoch minus element-set epoch, signed. A comparison beyond 1000 km is counted as lost: the public set is not on the file's trajectory at all. at_file_start takes each satellite once, at the first epoch of its own file, which is the only cut comparable between cycles. Both inputs are predictions; the operator's includes planned trajectory changes the public set cannot know about.

Snapshot 20260909T181011Z_e037a4cf1ccc. Evaluation every 360 minutes across each file's own record epochs. Public element sets come from Space-Track.org and are redistributed under Space-Track's blanket approval for basic space situational awareness data, with citation.

Operator ephemerides are predictions, not observations. Starlink is the only operator with public covariance; other operators enter via CelesTrak SupGP without covariance. Public GP data is too noisy to test sub-metre covariance; the self-consistency scoreboard measures prediction-versus-later-prediction. That scoreboard is not built yet. Inputs are archived by this project and witnessed by OpenTimestamps and the Wayback Machine; they are not re-fetchable from the source after one cycle. Every figure above carries the build time it was true at. Gapped or lost items are printed, never hidden.
